SCR-1.text: The first pass only decides whether there is enough relevant experience to keep reading; it is not a read of the whole career.
SCR-1.check: Is enough relevant experience visible at a first glance, from the top of page one?
SCR-1.label: Supported 2

SCR-2.text: Screeners read the most recent role first and judge fit mainly from recent, relevant experience.
SCR-2.check: Does the most recent role, at the top of the experience section, show the target role's core stack and kind of problem? Is the experience in reverse date order?
SCR-2.label: Consensus 3

SCR-3.text: The technical fit for the target role must be obvious on page one, without the reader searching for it.
SCR-3.check: Are the target role's must-have skills visible on page one? Would a recruiter hiring for that stack have to search through pages to find it?
SCR-3.label: Single source 1

ATS-1.text: Include the target role's keywords so recruiter searches and ATS filters find the CV.
ATS-1.check: Does the CV contain the job description's must-have terms in the same wording?
ATS-1.label: Single source 1

ATS-2.text: Write the CV for a human reader, not for the ATS; keyword lists without context make it unreadable.
ATS-2.check: Are keywords embedded in statements about the work, or are there buzzword strings and stuffed keyword blocks?
ATS-2.label: Single source 1

ATS-3.text: Screeners use the ATS to screen out applicants who fail a hard requirement of the role, such as security clearance eligibility.
ATS-3.check: If the job has a hard requirement (clearance, eligibility, mandatory certification), does the CV state the candidate's status for it in plain words?
ATS-3.label: Single source 1

STR-1.text: Keep the CV focused; do not document every task from every job.
STR-1.check: Are older or less relevant roles cut down to the essentials? Does any role list routine duties at length?
STR-1.label: Consensus 3

STR-2.check: Count pages; compare with the recruiters' common range, minding the experience each range was given for.
STR-2.label: Contested range 4
STR-2.evidence: Contested range 4 (0F/4P, 0 report rejecting); JA 1 page (6 years of DevOps experience (CV#01): 1 page; 8 years of mobile experience (CV#02): 1 page; 10 years as a data analyst (CV#04): 1 page), JB 2 to 5 pages, SB 2 pages (junior with little experience: 1 page; very experienced engineer, CTO or VP: at least 2 pages), TW 2 to 4 pages (junior or mid-level, one to two years of experience: 1 page; more than 10 years of experience: 3 to 4 pages); common none

measure.question: How long should the CV be?

SB: very experienced engineer, CTO or VP
TW: junior or mid-level, one to two years of experience

measure.text: JA 1 page (6 years of DevOps experience (CV#01): 1 page; 8 years of mobile experience (CV#02): 1 page; 10 years as a data analyst (CV#04): 1 page), JB 2 to 5 pages, SB 2 pages (junior with little experience: 1 page; very experienced engineer, CTO or VP: at least 2 pages), TW 2 to 4 pages (junior or mid-level, one to two years of experience: 1 page; more than 10 years of experience: 3 to 4 pages); common none

STR-3.text: Use a plain layout the reader can navigate quickly; fancy graphics add nothing.
STR-3.check: Are there graphics, icons, skill bars, heavy colors or multi-column designs that slow down skimming?
STR-3.label: Consensus 3

STR-4.text: Open the CV with a few tailored sentences saying who you are, what you specialize in and why you fit the role.
STR-4.check: Is there a short summary at the top? Is it specific to the target role, or generic?
STR-4.label: Supported 2

ACH-1.text: Under each role, describe the problem, the candidate's personal contribution and the result, not a list of technologies or responsibilities.
ACH-1.check: Does each recent role say what was built, what the candidate personally did and what changed? Flag bullets that are only technology names or duties.
ACH-1.label: Consensus 4

SKL-1.text: A technology list on page one shows the required skill set at a glance.
SKL-1.check: Is there a skills or technologies section on page one?
SKL-1.label: Single source 1

SKL-2.text: Do not repeat a full technology list under every role; name technologies in the context of the work.
SKL-2.check: Do role entries end with long tech lists that repeat the skills section?
SKL-2.label: Contested 1-1

GAP-1.text: A gap is not a problem in itself; show what was done during it to stay current (learning, projects).
GAP-1.check: For any gap of several months, does the CV show learning, projects or other activity in it?
GAP-1.label: No support

REG-1.text: Make the candidate's location and right-to-work status obvious.
REG-1.check: Does the CV header state the current location and the right to work for the target country (or the visa held)?
REG-1.label: No support

REG-2.text: Do not state a need for visa sponsorship on the CV.
REG-2.check: Does the CV say the candidate needs sponsorship?
REG-2.label: Single source 1

CHN-1.text: Use referrals, networking and short tailored messages alongside applications; they get the CV read more carefully.
CHN-1.check: Not a CV check; recommend it when the candidate relies only on cold applications.
CHN-1.label: No support

CHN-2.text: Keep the LinkedIn profile complete and active, consistent with the CV.
CHN-2.check: Does the profile have a photo, full job history, a bio and some activity, matching the CV?
CHN-2.label: No support

CHN-3.text: Skip a generic cover letter unless the employer asks for one; anything written should be short and specific to the company.
CHN-3.check: Is there a generic cover letter about passion and hard work? If a letter is required, is it short and specific?
CHN-3.label: Supported 2

SCR-4.text: Time a screener spends on the first pass of a CV, in seconds.
SCR-4.check: Context for the first-pass rules: what must be visible within that time (SCR-1, SCR-3).
SCR-4.label: Contested range 2
SCR-4.evidence: Contested range 2 (2F/0P, 0 report rejecting); JA 10 seconds (checking a CV for the required tech stack: 5 to 10 seconds), JB 30 seconds (first pass: 30 seconds); common none

measure.text: JA 10 seconds (checking a CV for the required tech stack: 5 to 10 seconds), JB 30 seconds (first pass: 30 seconds); common none

ATS-4.text: Screening decisions are made by people reading the CV; the ATS is not relied on to judge candidates.
ATS-4.check: Context for ATS advice: write for the human reader and do not trade readability for keyword density.

SCR-5.text: A recruiter has to justify internally why each candidate introduced to the hiring manager is worth meeting.
SCR-5.check: Could a recruiter take two or three concrete reasons to shortlist from the CV?
SCR-5.label: Single source 1

X-INT.text: Interview-stage advice (phone screens and later interviews).
X-INT.label: Consensus 4

X-VOL.text: Application volume and targeting of employers.
X-VOL.label: Consensus 3

ACH-2.text: Under each role, name the business domain (such as fintech or healthcare) and the end customers the work served.
ACH-2.check: Does each recent role say which domain the work was in and who the end customers were?
ACH-2.label: Single source 1

CHN-4.text: Share of a recruiter's placements that came from referrals, in percent.
CHN-4.check: Context for CHN-1, how much hiring runs through referrals rather than applications.
CHN-4.label: Single source 1
CHN-4.evidence: Single source 1 (1F/0P, 0 report rejecting); JB 70 percent (early career: 70 percent)

measure.question: What share of a recruiter's placements comes from referrals?

SCR-6.text: Screeners look at where the candidate has worked (the employers) on the first look.
SCR-6.check: Are employer names easy to spot in each role heading?
SCR-6.label: Supported 2

SCR-7.text: Screeners look at the candidate's tech stack on the first look.
SCR-7.check: Is the stack of each recent role easy to find, and does it match the target role's core stack?
SCR-7.label: Consensus 3

STR-5.text: Include education (university and degree, with a notable grade such as merit or distinction), even when the degree is not computer science.
STR-5.check: Is there an education section with university, degree and any notable grade?
STR-5.label: No support

SEN-1.text: For startup roles, give each employer's stage and funding (seed, series A, VC backing, amount raised) and the tenure through it.
SEN-1.check: For startup applications, does each startup employer show its stage or funding?

SEN-2.text: Visible progression within a company, such as a promotion to senior, is a positive signal.
SEN-2.check: Are promotions shown as separate titles with dates under the same employer?

GAP-2.text: Explain gaps and short stints on the CV; unexplained ones are a red flag.

SKL-3.text: Show where each listed technology was used (in which role or project).

ACH-3.text: Lead each achievement with the outcome in plain English, then the technical detail, so a non-technical screener can follow it.
ACH-3.check: Does each bullet state the problem or result in plain words before the technology names?

ACH-4.text: Side projects and hackathons show genuine interest in the work and help a CV.
ACH-4.check: Are relevant side projects or hackathons listed?
ACH-4.label: Consensus 3

SEN-3.text: For startup roles, state zero-to-one product building experience explicitly.
SEN-3.check: For startup applications, if the candidate built a product from scratch, does the CV say so in those words?
SEN-3.label: Single source 1

SEN-4.text: For startup roles, a big-company background can count against the candidate unless the CV shows startup-like work (greenfield projects, shipping fast).
SEN-4.check: For a startup application from a large company, does the CV describe the team's pace and greenfield work?
SEN-4.label: Single source 1

CHN-5.text: Include a LinkedIn URL on the CV.
CHN-5.check: Is there a LinkedIn URL in the header?
CHN-5.label: Single source 1

CHN-6.text: Link GitHub only when it shows real activity; an empty GitHub can hurt.
CHN-6.check: If a GitHub link is present, does the profile show recent contributions?
CHN-6.label: Supported 2

CHN-7.text: Recruiters use LinkedIn to find candidates and check their experience; without a profile, screening is harder.
CHN-7.check: Context for CHN rules; flag a candidate with no LinkedIn profile.
CHN-7.label: No support

SKL-4.text: Show on the CV how AI tools are used in the development workflow.
SKL-4.check: Does the CV mention concrete use of AI coding tools in daily work?
SKL-4.label: Supported 2

RED-2.text: Missing a core skill of the role's stack is a rejection.
RED-2.check: Compare the job's core stack (language, main frameworks) with the CV; a missing core item is critical.
RED-2.label: Consensus 3

STR-6.text: Tailor the CV to each job, so the skills and experience the job asks for are apparent.
STR-6.check: Does the CV emphasize what this job's description asks for?
STR-6.label: Single source 1

SKL-5.text: Screeners weigh the core stack (language, frontend and backend frameworks) most; cloud providers such as AWS and GCP are treated as interchangeable.

REG-3.text: Give contact details in the header, including email and a phone number with the correct country code.

REG-3.label: Supported 2

REG-4.text: Screeners compare the candidate's location with the job's location, including the phone number's country and the distance to the office.

REG-4.label: No support

REG-5.text: If the candidate would relocate, say so on the CV (for example "happy to relocate").
REG-5.check: For a candidate abroad, does the CV state willingness to relocate?
REG-5.label: Single source 1

RED-3.text: Everything on the CV must be accurate and defensible; a line the candidate cannot back up is an instant rejection.
RED-3.check: Is any claim on the CV unsupported or likely to fall apart under a question (watch AI-written lines)?
RED-3.label: Single source 1

REG-6.text: Working English good enough to follow technical requirements and product direction is expected.
REG-6.check: If the CV has a language section, is English stated at a working level?
REG-6.label: Supported 2

SKL-6.text: Startups look for breadth across the stack rather than a narrow focus on one layer.
SKL-6.check: For startup applications, does the CV show work across frontend, backend and data, not one layer only?
SKL-6.label: Supported 2

SCR-8.text: Screeners notice the CV's formatting first, before reading its content.
SCR-8.check: Context for STR-3; at a glance, does the CV look clean and easy to read?
SCR-8.label: Single source 1

SCR-9.text: Screeners look at the candidate's job titles early in the first pass; a title may differ from the target role's wording.
SCR-9.check: Do the job titles make the kind of role obvious?
SCR-9.label: Single source 1

SCR-10.text: Screeners look for experience in the employer's industry (such as finance for a financial firm) when the hiring manager asks for it.
SCR-10.check: If the job ad or manager asks for industry experience, is it visible in the role headings or company context?
SCR-10.label: Single source 1

RED-4.text: Hiring managers spot AI-written CVs quickly and do not want to see too much AI in a CV.

STR-7.text: Between each job title and its bullet points, add a short paragraph on the company and the work (what the company does, its sector, the team, the main problems and how they were solved).

STR-8.text: Length of the company context paragraph under each role, in lines.

measure.question: How long should the company context paragraph under each role be?

CHN-8.text: Keep GitHub up to date, because hiring managers sometimes look it up even when the CV does not link it.
CHN-8.check: If the candidate has a public GitHub, is it current?
CHN-8.label: Single source 1

ACH-5.text: List coding contest ratings or algorithm practice (such as LeetCode or HackerRank) when the candidate has them, briefly and highlighted, for example in a side column.
ACH-5.check: If the candidate has such a rating, is it on the CV without taking much space?
ACH-5.label: Single source 1

SKL-7.text: Hiring managers want candidates with some exposure to agentic development or AI tools, and do not want to hire anyone who is against AI.
SKL-7.check: Does the CV show any hands-on use of AI tools or agentic development?
SKL-7.label: Single source 1

CHN-9.text: Hiring managers usually open a GitHub link on the CV and browse the projects quickly.
CHN-9.check: Context for CHN-6 and CHN-8; if GitHub is linked, what will a quick browse show?
CHN-9.label: Supported 2

CHN-10.text: Use a standard job title (such as software engineer or senior data engineer) on LinkedIn and keep it consistent, because recruiters search by standard titles.
CHN-10.check: Is the LinkedIn headline title a standard one, with any creative title only after it?
CHN-10.label: Single source 1

REG-7.text: Do not put a photo or pictures of any kind on the CV.
REG-7.check: Is there a photo, logo or other picture on the CV?
REG-7.label: Single source 1

STR-9.text: Keep every past employer and its dates on the CV; do not remove older jobs to look less experienced.
STR-9.check: Are any employers or dates missing from the work history?
STR-9.label: Single source 1

STR-10.text: Years of work history to describe in detail on the CV.
STR-10.check: How far back do detailed role descriptions go? Compare with the recruiters' common range; older roles can be listed without detail (STR-1).
STR-10.label: Single source 1

STR-12.text: Leave references off the CV; they add nothing.

SKL-9.text: Do not list soft skills in a section of their own; show them in the summary and the bullet points.
